Abstract: Executable specifications make software assumptions explicit and checkable, yet their role in quantum information and machine learning (QIML) remains underexplored. We argue that executable specifications should be treated as first-class artifacts for independent verification and validation (IV&V) of QIML systems. Static analysis, testing, simulation, and runtime checking can provide evidence about QIML behavior, while Design by Contract shows that selected quantum-state, measurement, and statistical properties can be expressed as checkable conditions. However, adapting existing methods for specification inference and assessment from conventional and machine-learning software to QIML raises several challenges, notably limited evidence for deriving generalizable specifications, cross-stage and probabilistic behavior, repository-scale reasoning across hybrid workflows, and weak behavioral oracles. We characterize these challenges and identify research directions for QIML corpora, specification semantics, repository-level analysis, and specification assessment.
items.author: Ragib Shahariar Ayon, Shibbir Ahmed

items.title: From Prompt Engineering to Programmatic Prompting: Toward a Software Engineering Discipline for Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.09896v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The practice of instructing large language models (LLMs) through natural-language prompts has, in the span of a few years, migrated from an interactive curiosity to a load-bearing component of production software. Yet the vocabulary, tooling, and mental models of the field remain anchored in its interactive origins: we still speak of "prompt engineering" as though the crafting of a single well-worded instruction were the central problem. This paper argues for a categorical distinction. Prompt engineering, we contend, is an interaction technique - a human-computer interaction skill for eliciting desired behavior from a model in a conversational or exploratory setting. Programmatic prompting, by contrast, is an engineering discipline governing the behavioral interface between software systems and language models: the construction, composition, versioning, testing, and maintenance of prompts as first-class software artifacts embedded in larger systems. Conflating the two has produced brittle applications, unrepeatable evaluations, and an accumulation of prompt debt. We make three contributions: (1) a definition of programmatic prompting; (2) a systematic differentiation of programmatic prompting from prompt engineering, prompt tuning, fine-tuning, and general LLM application development; and (3) an account of prompt debt that distinguishes the self-admitted debt measurable in code from the silent debt that surfaces only as incidents, and identifies its economic cause. Our thesis is simple to state and consequential to accept: prompt engineering is an interaction technique; programmatic prompting is an engineering discipline.
items.author: Sebastian Dingler

items.title: Mutation Testing for Multi-Agent Workflows
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.09895v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are defined by explicit workflows, agents, tools, tool-access rules, and delegation paths. Most evaluations, however, report end-to-end task success rather than whether a test suite can detect faults in this coordination structure, such as a removed delegation, a silently removed restriction, a misrouted tool edge, or a faulty tool implementation. We adapt mutation analysis to this setting, fourteen operators in four families (delegation, allowed-tool, restriction, agent/instruction) perturb a normalized workflow manifest, and three kill criteria score whether a suite catches the change, namely K-Struct on the observed coordination, KOutcome on the task verdict or step sequence, and K-Safety on a forbidden tool call. Every criterion is evaluated by executing each suite against the original and the mutant through the OpenAI Agents SDK, with k=3 repeats and a majority vote. On ten OpenAI Agents SDK-derived workflows (49 reachable agents, 47 tools, 403 obligations), the evaluation executes 29,601 agent runs over a pool of 1,084 mutants. We use T-Struct only as a full-obligation reference point (MSstrict=1.000 under all three criteria) and measure how much the baseline suites miss, the bestperforming one (T-Dev*) reaches 0.717 (K-Struct) and only 0.559 (K-Safety). Restriction-removal (RES-REM) is the least detected fault for the baselines (0.19 to 0.28 vs 1.000). Executing the suites also allows the obligation-preserving operators (TOOL-FAULT, AG-SWAP, AG-PROMPTDROP) to be evaluated. A manifest-only oracle would not witness these changes. In this setting, tasksuccess- style suites catch only about half of permission violations.
items.author: Nafiseh Kahani, Mojtaba Bagherzadeh

items.title: SlotGuard: Stop Oversharing Private Local Context in LLM Agent Transcripts
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.17147v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: LLM agents can expose private local context (e.g., paths, emails) and credentials (e.g., API keys) as agent observations (e.g., tool outputs, shell logs, and file reads) are appended to provider-bound transcripts. Existing placeholder redaction is brittle: it can miss embedded or cross-turn references, over-redact benign lookalikes, and destroy the structure useful for reasoning. We present SlotGuard, a local transcript boundary that can hide sensitive data while retaining agents' performance. SlotGuard rewrites structural bindings as typed, suffix-aware slots, replaces secrets with format-preserving synthetic values, links cross-turn references with a lightweight session graph, and restores raw values only inside the trusted runtime. On controlled repository-oriented agent transcripts, SlotGuard removes all 20,814 annotated structurally sensitive characters across 9,229 paths and reduces credential leakage to 0.0% across 852 planted values. It remains close to raw-transcript task success across four upstream models, while generic redaction drops to 2.5%. Deterministic transcript rewriting takes a median of 14.424 microseconds per agent turn, excluding the optional semantic detector. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/illinoisdata/SlotGuard.
items.author: Haocheng Xia, Yongjoo Park

items.title: LLM Watermarking as Big Data Provenance: A Deployment-Oriented Systematization
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.10103v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) generate and transform content at scale, reliable attribution becomes an increasingly important requirement for big data provenance. Although numerous watermarking methods have been proposed, existing evaluations predominantly emphasize sample-level detectability and robustness, leaving deployment requirements such as serving efficiency, population-scale false positives, multi-key attribution, and long-term verification less systematically examined. This paper presents a deployment-oriented systematization of LLM watermarking through the five Vs of big data: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, and Value. We classify representative watermarking methods across four dimensions: insertion point, verification authority, operational state, and adversarial threat model. We further map these methods to four deployment workloads: online generation, streaming detection, transformation pipelines, and ecosystem governance. Our synthesis identifies recurring limitations, including dependencies on generation-time access, additional inference overhead, sensitivity to downstream transformations, and incomplete reporting of calibration and lifecycle compatibility. Based on these findings, we propose workload-specific evaluation requirements covering statistical reliability, throughput, utility, robustness, and governance. This framework connects watermark design choices to practical deployment constraints and provides guidance for selecting and evaluating provenance mechanisms in large-scale data ecosystems.
items.author: Huy Phan, Kieu Dang, Ojaswi Dulal, Aiham AL Shukairi, Abby Shine, Chase Garner, Phung Lai

items.title: JU\'A -- A Benchmark for Information Retrieval in Brazilian Legal Text Collections
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.06098v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Legal information retrieval in Portuguese remains difficult to evaluate systematically because available datasets differ widely in document type, query style, and relevance definition. We present JU\'A, a public benchmark for Brazilian legal retrieval designed to support more reproducible and comparable evaluation across heterogeneous legal collections. More broadly, JU\'A is intended not only as a benchmark, but as a continuous evaluation infrastructure for Brazilian legal IR, combining shared protocols, common ranking metrics, fixed splits when applicable, and a public leaderboard. The benchmark covers jurisprudence retrieval as well as broader legislative, regulatory, and question-driven legal search. We evaluate lexical, dense, and BM25-based reranking pipelines, including a domain-adapted Qwen embedding model fine-tuned on JU\'A-aligned supervision. Results show that the benchmark is sufficiently heterogeneous to distinguish retrieval paradigms and reveal substantial cross-dataset trade-offs. Domain adaptation yields its clearest gains on the supervision-aligned JU\'A-Juris subset, while BM25 remains highly competitive on other collections, especially in settings with strong lexical and institutional phrasing cues. Overall, JU\'A provides a practical evaluation framework for studying legal retrieval across multiple Brazilian legal domains under a common benchmark design.
items.author: Jayr Pereira, Leandro Fernandes, Erick de Brito, Roberto Lotufo, Luiz Bonifacio

items.title: Measuring Collapse and Correction in Homogeneous-Panel LLM Debate
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.35279v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) debate is often evaluated by whether final answers improve, but a changed answer is not necessarily a better one: the same discussion can correct an initially wrong majority or collapse an initially correct one. Standard final-accuracy evaluations conflate these opposing transitions. We introduce an auditable protocol for homogeneous debate on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) that records each run as a transition ledger over collapse, correction, onset, and signed intervention utility. On 6,925 MMLU-Pro debates, the protocol records 253 collapses together with the corrections that offset them, and the correction side changes how interventions should be judged. Replay experiments reveal the central tradeoff: freezing every debate prevents 251 collapses but loses 804 corrections under equal weights, and a leave-one-model-out probe-gated freeze that is tuned for net utility never fires, so collapse prevention alone can recommend the wrong policy. A compact pre-debate 8-probe screen is a triage signal: its unadjusted family-level association with conditional-collapse risk is high (G=7, Spearman $\rho$ = 0.893, exact two-sided p = 0.0123), but initial-majority accuracy is a close comparator ($\rho$ = -0.821; family partial $\rho$ = 0.767, p = 0.0877), so we do not treat it as calibrated or capability-adjusted prediction. Round-level traces localize many collapses to the first debate round, where early disagreement can precede both collapses and corrections. Reasoning-mode models, including one model at two reasoning-effort levels, also show both collapses and corrections. We release replayable schemas, coders, audits, cost cards, and zero-API rebuild scripts so future model rows can be compared under the same denominators and signed utility ledger.
items.author: Xin Li, Mengbing Liu, Chau Yuen

items.title: Rewarding Novel Deductions: Solver-guided Process Supervision for Logical Reasoning
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.34660v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Logical reasoning remains a major challenge for large language models (LLMs), particularly on structured problems that require precise constraint tracking, consistency preservation, and multi-step deduction. This challenge is especially acute for small-scale LLMs, which are more prone to producing inconsistent, redundant, or brittle reasoning trajectories. Existing approaches for improving logical reasoning largely optimize for final-answer correctness, providing only weak supervision over the intermediate reasoning process. In this work, we propose SPRING: (Solver-guided Process Rewards for Novel LogIcal ReasoNing Step Generation). SPRING uses an SMT solver as a training-time verifier of intermediate reasoning steps to provide process-level supervision. It introduces the notion of a novel reasoning step, namely, a step that is logically valid, consistent with the evolving reasoning state, and not already implied by previously accepted non-contradictory deductions. Based on this solver-based assessment, it designs process rewards that encourage novel inferential progress while penalizing contradictory and uninformative reasoning steps. Evaluation across three logical reasoning benchmarks: ZebraLogic, AR-LSAT, and Knights and Knaves, and four LLMs shows that SPRING consistently outperforms base LLMs, outcome-only reward baselines, and Logic-LM. On ZebraLogic, SPRING improves puzzle accuracy by up to 49.71 and 15.43 points over the base LLM and strongest outcome-only baseline, respectively. On AR-LSAT, it improves overall accuracy by up to 64.43 and 11.39 percentage points over the base LLM and strongest outcome-only baseline, respectively. On Knights and Knaves, SPRING achieves up to 93.14 puzzle accuracy and 96.05 person accuracy.
items.author: Muhammad Asif Ali, Wenqing Wang, Huan Wang, Mohammad Raza

items.title: ToolSearcher: Optimizing Tool Selection at Scale via Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.30906v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language processing but struggle to interact with external environments. Tool learning provides a promising way to extend LLMs into actionable agents, where tool selection is a critical prerequisite for successful tool use. Existing work often assumes a small or predefined set of tools, leaving large-scale tool selection underexplored. Real-world repositories contain a vast and diverse array of tools, making it difficult for LLMs to effectively search, distinguish, and compose tools under context-length constraints. We identify large-scale tool selection as a new challenge for agentic reinforcement learning, highlighting that existing RL methods for knowledge-based question answering are inadequate for selecting tools while considering compatibility. To address this challenge, we propose ToolSearcher, a novel RL framework for effective multi-turn search and fine-grained optimization in large-scale tool selection. Specifically, we introduce category-constrained tool discrimination to improve the model's ability to distinguish functionally similar tools, event-level search modeling to explicitly optimize the discovery of target tools during multi-turn search, and trajectory-aligned credit allocation to provide fine-grained reward signals for different stages of the search-selection process. Extensive experiments on large-scale tool selection benchmarks demonstrate that ToolSearcher consistently outperforms a set of strong baselines in challenging settings involving iterative search and complex tool composition.
items.author: Zhenlong Dai, Xujie Song, Zitong Wang, Tong Niu, Jian liu, Weiqiang Wang, Xiu Tang, Sai Wu, Chang Yao, Jingyuan Chen

items.title: Enhancing Assessment of Self-Consistency in LLM Explanations using Perturbation Strength
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.30849v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Prior work has examined the self-consistency of LLM-generated explanations using surface-level perturbation methods. However, the strength of these perturbations is not explicitly measured and controlled. In this work, we propose an LLM-as-a-judge approach to measure perturbation strength in a unified manner across input and CoT perturbations. We then evaluate the self-consistency in explanations generated from various LLMs under controlled strength conditions, ensuring a fair comparison across perturbation types. Experiments show that our proposed LLM-based perturbation strength measure outperforms other embedding- and probability-based approaches and that input perturbations generally affect LLMs more strongly than CoT perturbations. Our work suggests that judgments about a model's self-consistency is fair only within the same perturbation type.
items.author: Phuong Q. Le, Kemal Kurniawan, Jey Han Lau

items.title: PACE-dLLM: Elastic Block Decoding via Confidence Cliff Estimation for Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.26249v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs), such as LLaDA and Dream, have become competitive with autoregressive (AR) LLMs in generation quality while supporting native parallel decoding. A standard acceleration strategy is block-wise decoding, where each forward pass predicts a block of length B and commits high-confidence tokens. Confidence-threshold commitment adapts which tokens are accepted, but a fixed B still constrains the prediction scope. Existing horizon policies use manually chosen sizes, volatility statistics, or candidate-boundary scores. We instead use the model's own per-step confidence: in-window confidence typically follows a context-dependent cliff, providing a direct signal for adapting the look-ahead horizon. In this work, we propose PACE-dLLM, which refits this parametric cliff periodically in closed form, sets the next horizon at a shared confidence anchor, and retains confidence-threshold token commitment. Under a saturated-yield abstraction with iid, policy-independent monotone profiles, the oracle horizon is the smallest attaining maximal per-pass yield and improves the asymptotic forward-pass rate when fixed blocks undershoot it with positive probability. On four reasoning and code benchmarks across two open-source dLLM backbones, PACE-dLLM achieves the best average accuracy among the evaluated decoders on both backbones, with average throughput speedups of 5.23x on LLaDA and 3.06x on Dream (up to 8.52x on LLaDA MATH) over the unaccelerated semi-AR baseline, advancing the quality-throughput Pareto frontier.
items.author: Xiaocheng Lu, Shuhan Guo, Ziyue Ma, Jie Zhang, Jian Liu, Jingcai Guo, Haoxuan Che, Song Guo

items.title: ScienceIDE: Turning World's Scientific Codebase into Agent Learnable Environments
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.19134v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scientific code repositories encode decades of human knowledge in executable models, methods, and tools. Yet fragmented toolchains, implicit domain conventions, and specialized correctness criteria make this knowledge difficult to convert into reliable learning experience-a challenge we call the scientific experience bottleneck. We introduce ScienceIDE, infrastructure for turning the world's scientific code into programmable environments for scientific agents. Guided by expert-defined scientific cases and acceptance criteria, agents transform repositories into executable environments that support task generation, execution, and scientific verification. These environments provide a shared foundation for supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and evaluation. Using verified interaction trajectories, we train PhAI-IDE-72B/9B/4B. The model family shows gains in held-out scientific-code repair and across selected general-purpose benchmarks in code, reasoning, and knowledge, providing evidence of positive transfer from scientific experience to broader capabilities. ScienceIDE lays the foundation for an integrated workspace for agent learning and scientific practice, making humanity's scientific software a shared substrate for developing scientific intelligence. Code: https://github.com/aitofound/ScienceIDE
items.author: Hejia Geng, Zesen Huang, Haoyang Li, Wenbin Li, Koutian Wu, Zihan Zhou, Yuanbo Pang, Weihao Liu, Zigong Xu, Zhiping Li, Zongzheng Zhang, Chuanfei Dong, Jiankai Sun, Tianzhe Zheng, Fengyu Xie, Yue Ma, Yueheng Shi, Junkai Wang, Tong Xie, Zonglin Di, Xianrong Liu, Qucheng Gao, Yimin Liu, Jiaming Pan, Sheng Huang, Xiao-Han Ma, Lanqing Yuan, Zhenlin Zhu, Ziang Liu, Ziyang Xu, Kangkai Liang, Jiayi Xian, Zehong Zhao, Taigao Ma, Fuming Chang, Yuanzhe Hu, Liuwei Xu, Xianzhe Tang, Jingxu Xie, Peijin Zhang, Qiang Gao, Chengyi Xing, Zhe Zhao, Xi Wang, Leo Wang, Fang Wu, Jiacheng Ge, Weixuan Liao, Jungang Chen, Shuozhe Li, Yi Daniel Lu, Xu Pan, Shuhang Lin, Peihan Tu, Nan Liu, Zelin Tan, Yunze Xiao, Hao Xiao, Yaopeng Xing, Xing Meng, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang

items.title: A Hybrid Hierarchical 1D-CNN-BiLSTM Framework for Extractive Summarization of Biomedical and Clinical Text
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.13481v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models have made abstractive summarization remarkably fluent, but fluency has come at a cost. Models trained to generate freely over long documents may hallucinate, producing summaries that read well but drift from what the source actually says. This risk is especially serious in biomedical and clinical text, where fabricated details can have serious consequences. We address this by removing free-form generation from the pipeline rather than trying to constrain it. Our Hybrid Hierarchical CNN-LSTM Summarizer reframes summarization as extractive sentence selection: a stacked, multi-kernel convolutional network progressively refines contextual representations, while a bidirectional LSTM models long-range dependencies across the document. A lightweight scoring head predicts sentence importance using binary cross-entropy supervision. For PubMed, a document-adaptive mean-plus-standard-deviation threshold with a Top-3 fallback determines extraction; clinical evaluations instead use a fixed top-30\% sentence-selection policy. Because output sentences are copied verbatim, the framework prevents source-external generation, although omissions and contextual inaccuracies remain possible. Evaluated on PubMed and transferred without clinical fine-tuning to MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV BHC, the model demonstrates competitive extractive summarization performance, with threshold and component ablations supporting adaptive extraction and the combined CNN--BiLSTM architecture. Clinical factuality analysis further highlights limitations in preserving important findings and negations. These results suggest that structural constraints offer a promising direction for source-grounded biomedical summarization, while emphasizing the importance of clinical completeness and contextual fidelity.
items.author: Saad Bin Ather, Muhammad Saif, Ali Hassan Khan, Manzer Abbas, Hajra Waheed

items.title: Who Pays More for Safety? Measuring the Disparate Cost of Safety Alignment across Languages
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.22490v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Safety alignment helps models adhere to human values, but it often reduces response utility. We ask a critical but understudied question: Does safety alignment impose the cost equally across language groups? To answer this, we introduce a rigorous protocol to measure the utility loss imposed solely by safety alignment, which we term Safety Cost. Through direct pairwise comparisons between safety-aligned models and their unaligned counterparts, we find a systematic inequity: non-English users consistently bear a higher Safety Cost than English users. We further identify three underlying patterns. First, multiple languages lie in a double-penalty zone, experiencing both weaker safety protection and larger utility loss. Second, certain languages exhibit apparent utility gains that are in fact a consequence of safety filters failing to engage. Third, even high-resource languages pay a larger Safety Cost than English to reach the same level of safety. We show that these disparities arise from both explicit refusals and implicit qualitative differences across multiple dimensions. By accurately measuring the disparate effects of safety alignment, our findings expose a systematic disparity in current safety alignment practices.
items.author: Chanwoong Yoon, Jungsoo Park, Alan Ritter

items.title: Auditing Exposure to Harmful Content on TikTok using Multimodal Language Models: A Cross-National, Age-Stratified Study
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.17583v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Online video platforms can expose young users to harmful content, but independent audits remain difficult because video annotation is costly and moderation judgments vary across languages. We audit TikTok in France, Italy, and Sweden with sockpuppet accounts representing four age personas (13, 16, 19, 40), collecting 36,971 videos from passive For-You-page scrolling and active sessions that scroll, search for harm keywords, and scroll again. To scale annotation, we validate four multimodal LLMs against native-speaker labels on a 300-video reference set. Gemini 2.5 Flash with eight sampled frames plus text performs best (aggregate kappa = 0.42), at half the per-call cost of native-video upload, and we apply it to a 10% sample for approximately \$50 in total API spend across both modalities. Keyword search returns 35-56% harmful content, a 1.5-7.5x increase over the scrolling baseline in ten of twelve country-age combinations; the spike is temporary and flattens the age differences observed in France and Sweden. Under passive scrolling, Italy has the highest harm rate at every age, with Italian age-19 reaching 48.6%. Overall, MLLM-based auditing offers a scalable approach for cross-national youth-safety audits, while provider safety filters (1.1% refusal rate) under-count the most explicit harms.
items.author: Hamidreza Saffari, Francesco Pierri

items.title: DonorRank: Donor Language Selection for Low-Resource Cross-Lingual Speech Recognition
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.11441v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Low-resource automatic speech recognition (ASR) often relies on cross-lingual transfer from higher-resource languages due to limited availability of transcribed speech. However, selecting an effective donor language is a nontrivial issue, particularly in settings with spontaneous speech, linguistic variation, and uneven resource availability. We present DonorRank, a learning-to-rank framework that uses linguistic and dataset-level features along with previously observed transfer outcomes to predict promising donor languages for zero-shot ASR. We evaluate DonorRank on two multilingual speech corpora of Indic and African languages. DonorRank produces informative donor rankings across both collections, outperforming common heuristics in the more closely related Indic setting while remaining competitive in the more linguistically diverse African setting. Our analysis reveals that effective donors are not always the closest linguistic relatives and that the most informative predictors vary across language collections. These findings highlight the value of learned donor selection for prioritizing transfer experiments in low-resource ASR. We will also release all of our evaluation results, feature matrices for all languages, scripts for training the DonorRank framework, and pairwise transfer performance matrices for our datasets.
items.author: Akriti Dhasmana, Aarohi Srivastava, David Chiang

items.title: Decomposition-Induced Context-Memory Conflict: An Instruction-Induced Failure and a Probing Case Study
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.10627v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Decompose-then-verify pipelines (FActScore-style fact-checkers, hallucination detectors) first split a passage into atomic claims and treat this step as neutral preprocessing. We ask whether a decomposer can substitute its own parametric belief for what the passage says, producing a claim that contradicts its source, and call this Decomposition-Induced Context-Memory Conflict (DI-CC). On biographies with a deliberately altered year, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct does so in 4.3% of claims when the instruction licenses self-correction, but in only 0.2-0.5% under a neutral instruction, a FActScore-style few-shot prompt, a "use only the passage" instruction, a formatting instruction, or a knowledge-filling instruction (an upper bound: in the neutral and FActScore-style runs only 1 of 13 flagged claims is a real override); context-aware decoding removes only half. DI-CC here is therefore instruction-induced. We then test whether a linear probe trained only on classical context-memory conflict data (NQ-Swap) detects DI-CC zero-shot. Its AUC is high (up to 0.94 against legit claims, 0.98 under a position- and instruction-matched control), but random directions reach AUCs between about 0.1 and 0.9 on these contrasts, probes fit directly on the claims reach 0.96-1.00 everywhere (even on a control that separates only the text variant), and after multiplicity correction the NQ-Swap probe beats random directions only at the last layer, and only for two of three random-direction families. A direct NLI check between source and claim reaches AUC 0.998. High probe AUC on such small contrasts is not evidence of a shared mechanism without nulls, and two pitfalls, pair leakage in probe training and duplicated BOS tokens, can change such conclusions.
items.author: Yu-Feng Yen

items.title: Tevatron-Elastic: A Unified Abstraction for Training Elastic Retrievers and Rerankers
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.08809v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A single model scale challenges the flexibility of a production retrieval system: some settings need it faster, others need a smaller index, and the right trade-off changes with the workload. In the context of information retrieval (IR), a transformer-based model can be made smaller in three ways --- using fewer layers, passing fewer tokens through the upper layers, or producing a shorter embedding --- and each way saves a different resource. These options have been studied in isolation, each as its own method with its own code and training setup, which makes them hard to combine or adapt to a new model. In this work, we present Tevatron-Elastic to bring all three under one unified abstraction: a single object names any size the model can run at, and a short schedule lists the sizes to train. Training then produces one checkpoint that serves all of those sizes, and at deployment the user has the liberty to pick any of them. The same abstraction covers both retrievers and rerankers and both encoder and decoder models, as it works through interfaces that Hugging Face transformers already expose; adding a new backbone can be a configuration change rather than a model rewrite. Prior methods --- Matryoshka embeddings, early exit, 2D Matryoshka (Starbucks), and layerwise token compression (LTC) --- become special cases of our unified abstraction. With Tevatron-Elastic, we also propose a new elastic algorithm Matryoshka~LTC (MLTC) to jointly train several token-compression ratios in one retriever checkpoint. To validate our framework, we train 20 checkpoints across three backbones and two tasks: the quality curves are smooth, full-point quality remains close to that of models trained for a single size, and a controlled study confirms the wall-clock speedups. We release the framework and all checkpoints to support elastic retrieval research.
items.author: Yu Wang, Shengyao Zhuang, Xueguang Ma, Zongyu Wu, Jimmy Lin, Vivek Srikumar, Zhichao Xu

items.title: AWARE-FX: Auditable measurement of corporate foreign-exchange hedging disclosure
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.27611v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Corporate annual reports describe hedging through transactional, policy, accounting, and explicit non-use language. This study presents AWARE-FX, the foreign-exchange application of the Auditable Weak-supervision and Aggregation framework, for constructing traceable firm-year disclosure measures. Professional-source retrieval, evidence-state rules, channel classifiers, and top-three aggregation link each score to supporting passages. The application covers 24,909 Hong Kong firm-years from 2008-2025 and 543,527 candidate snippets. Evaluation combines weak-label held-out tests, three-seed encoder comparisons, a 2023-2025 temporal test, calibration diagnostics, selective prediction, and a stratified 300-snippet audit coded by one researcher. The paired temporal tests do not detect statistically significant differences between FinBERT and ModernBERT. The negation-aware lexicon has higher broad-task audit F1 than strict-gate FinBERT and Qwen3-8B, demonstrating that learned models do not uniformly improve on domain rules. At 80% temporal coverage, retained-sample F1 increases by 0.050-0.077, although the study does not measure human review time or deployment impact. Reproducible Qwen3-8B results show substantial variation across evidence channels. Linked exposure associations provide exploratory external validation, with sensitivity to the multiple-testing family. The scores measure detected hedging disclosure rather than hedge notional or causal effectiveness. The contribution is an evaluated measurement workflow with inspectable evidence and explicit validation limits. Independent duplicate annotation and retrieval-recall assessment remain necessary for stronger reliability claims.
items.author: Qi Wang

items.title: MJ: Multi-turn LLM Jailbreaking via Decomposed Credit Assignment
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.11070v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) operate in interactive multi-turn settings, making multi-turn jailbreaking a realistic threat model and an important setting for automated red teaming. A core challenge in learning multi-turn jailbreak attackers is credit assignment: different turns contribute differently to the final outcome, yet existing learning signals are often too coarse to identify their individual contributions.
  We propose decomposed credit GRPO (DC-GRPO), a unified turn-level credit assignment framework for Group Relative Policy Optimization in multi-turn jailbreak learning. DC-GRPO assigns a separate group-relative learning signal to each turn by combining immediate and future credit, avoiding the credit misassignment induced by broadcasting a single trajectory-level score across the dialogue. We instantiate this framework with static and dynamic weighting rules that differ in how the two credit sources are balanced while sharing the same turn-level structure.
  Across four victim LLMs and three benchmarks, DC-GRPO achieves up to 98.26% average ASR_5@3, substantially outperforming the state-of-the-art methods, including SEMA (86.58%) and TROJail (86.23%), demonstrating the effectiveness of our turn-level group-relative credit assignment.
  Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful content.
items.author: Junyoung Park, Namgyu Park, Sechan Lee, Yoon-Chan Jhi, Jihoon Cho, Sangdon Park

items.title: Smooth Scaling Laws Hide Stepwise Token Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.29858v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language model loss follows remarkably regular scaling laws over model and data size, yet it remains unclear why the aggregate loss should exhibit a power-law form. Existing explanations often attribute this regularity to a heavy-tailed spectrum of pattern difficulty in natural language, but this view has not been directly validated at token-level granularity in large-scale real-data training. We present a token-level framework that decomposes scaling laws into localized learning events of individual contextualized tokens. By fitting token loss trajectories with sigmoids, we show that token learning is concentrated in localized transitions, giving rise to a learning-time spectrum that dominates the scaling-law shape. Across more than one hundred pre-training runs on large and diverse real-language corpora with modern LLM architectures, scaling up to 6B parameters and 300B training tokens, the measured learning-time spectrum quantitatively reconstructs the validation loss derivative along the training-step $T$, data-scale $D$, and model-scale $M$ axes. We further show that the same signal is actionable: by reshaping the training distribution according to when tokens become learnable, we alter the optimization trajectory and achieve 11\% faster validation-loss reduction. These results provide direct empirical evidence that scaling laws are governed primarily by the distribution of token-level learning times, and that this distribution can be used not only to explain scaling behavior but also to improve training performance.
items.author: Pingjie Wang, Zechen Hu, Peiru Yang, Fu Guo, Debing Zhang

items.title: Are Multilingual Models Actually Improving? Revisiting Cross-Lingual Transfer
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.21954v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Cross-lingual transfer is a model's ability to generalize capabilities from well-represented source languages to under-represented target languages. Existing measures of a model's transfer strength conflate improvements in transfer with general improvements to accuracy in the source language. We advocate for an alternate metric that reliably captures transfer strength called Hardness Adjusted Transfer (HAT) Score, and use it to derive multiple insights on factors influencing transfer strength. Our analysis across twenty diverse language models and three popular mainstream multilingual benchmarks argues that 1) transfer in small models is not broken, 2) we are making slower than expected progress in cross-lingual transfer with model size, and 3) we have made clear progress over time.
items.author: Prasoon Bajpai, Eleftheria Briakou, Colin Cherry, Preethi Jyothi, Vihari Piratla

items.title: Contrastive-Difference CKA Reveals Concept-Specific Structural Alignment Across Language Model Architectures
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.16897v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Do language models encode the same prompted concepts in structurally compatible ways, beyond generic similarity induced by shared questions? We study contrastive-difference centered kernel alignment ($\mathrm{CKA}_{\Delta}$), which compares per-question activation differences between opposing concept instructions. A matched same-concept versus cross-concept comparison separates the question of concept-conditioned structure from the magnitude of representational similarity. Across four checkpoints and eight personality-related traits, a fixed-final-layer analysis gives mean same- and cross-trait $\mathrm{CKA}_{\Delta}$ of 0.7259 and 0.6828. Trait-label randomization detects correspondence conditional on this model and prompt set ($p=1/10001$, one-sided), but a model-and-trait-weighted 95% interval for the difference is $[-0.0330,0.1017]$, limiting broader generalization. Strict question-group holdouts retain high same-trait linear recoverability. More stringently, maps and preprocessing fitted on seven traits transfer a source polarity classifier for the eighth trait to handwritten test questions: mean affine and orthogonal accuracies are 88.10% and 88.57%, versus 47.70% for shuffled pairing. Performance varies substantially across traits and model directions. Synthetic controls show why moderate CKA and high affine accuracy alone do not establish functional equivalence. The results support a scoped diagnostic of concept-specific structure and held-out linear recoverability; they do not establish universal invariance or a robust advantage over raw CKA across architectures.
items.author: Xueping Gao

items.title: MAAM: Anchor-Preserving Compression and Contextual Calibration for Chinese Discriminatory Language Detection
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.09114v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Chinese discriminatory-language detection is challenging because harmful intent is often implicit and context-dependent. We propose MAAM (Myopia--Astigmatism Anchor Mechanism), a lightweight, model-agnostic framework inspired by functional visual blur: rather than preserving every token equally, MAAM retains discrimination-relevant semantic anchors and calibrates them with C--I--S contextual priors (Contextual Tone, Group Identity, and Stance Polarity). We also introduce ChLGBT, to our knowledge the first Chinese LGBT-focused discriminatory-language dataset, with 8,120 manually annotated samples and three ordinal labels: explicit bias, implicit bias, and emotional intensity. Across strong encoder baselines, MAAM improves all three prediction dimensions, with consistent gains in accuracy, F1, Brier score, and expected calibration error. Compared with frontier LLM baselines under zero-shot and few-shot prompting protocols, MAAM remains competitive while offering stronger compactness and stability. These results suggest that interpretable anchor preservation and contextual calibration provide a practical alternative to heavier model scaling for Chinese discriminatory-language assessment.
items.author: Yuxin Fu, Shijing Si

items.title: Hint-Guided Diversified Policy Optimization for LLM Reasoning
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.03021v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent developments in Large Language Models (LLMs) have showcased impressive reasoning capabilities, with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) being a promising enhancement strategy. However, existing reward mechanisms are constrained to the outcome-level correctness and lack explicit signals to guide the model to consider diverse solutions. In contrast, human problem solving typically involves evaluating multiple potential approaches and selecting the most reliable solution, a cognitive process that current RLVR frameworks do not explicitly incentivize. Inspired by this, we propose Hint-Guided Diversified Policy Optimization (HDPO), allowing the model to first list all potential candidate solution outlines as hints and then select the most reliable one for further reasoning. HDPO comprises two stages of Cold Start for Structured Reasoning and Hint-Guided Diversified Reinforcement Learning to incentivize the model to generate diverse and reliable solutions following the ``propose-select-think'' trajectory. Experimental results show that HDPO effectively boosts LLM reasoning and enhances the diversity of candidate solutions as well as the LLM's ability to identify reliable solutions.
items.author: Zhiyu Cao, Kaixin Wu, Mingjie Zhong, Peifeng Li, Can Ye, Qiaoming Zhu

items.title: Geometric Latent Reasoning Induces Shorter Generations in LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.02248v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models solve complex problems by generating lengthy chains of explicit reasoning tokens. While effective, this makes reasoning expensive, length-sensitive, and constrained to (discrete) natural language. While latent reasoning offers a continuous alternative, determining useful structures for intermediate latent states is an open challenge. In this paper, we formulate latent reasoning as a geometric path-approximation problem within the model's pretrained token-embedding space. We introduce Geometric Latent Reasoning (GLR), which uses a lightweight transition head to predict iterative direction updates in embedding space. Using textual chain-of-thought traces as anchors, GLR learns to approximate discrete reasoning trajectories while permitting continuous deviations from exact token embeddings. Evaluations on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using Qwen3 models reveal an emergent phenomenon: geometric latent reasoning induces substantially shorter generations without an explicit length objective. By replacing early explicit reasoning with continuous latent steps, models often reach correct answers using substantially fewer total generation steps. These findings suggest that continuous trajectories act as compact intermediate reasoning states, exposing a new tradeoff between latent computation budget, output length, and accuracy. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/idiap/GLR. The project page is available at: https://glr-llm.github.io/.
items.author: Shashi Kumar, Yacouba Kaloga, Petr Motlicek, Ina Kodrasi, Andrea Cavallaro

items.title: dMoE: dLLMs with Learnable Block Experts
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.30876v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models, offering competitive performance while naturally supporting parallel decoding. However, as dLLMs are increasingly integrated with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures to scale model capacity, a fundamental mismatch arises between block parallel decoding and token-level expert selection. Specifically, each dLLM forward pass processes multiple tokens with bidirectional dependencies, whereas conventional MoE layers route each token independently. This mismatch substantially increases the number of uniquely activated experts, making inference increasingly memory-bound. To address this, we propose dMoE, a simple yet effective block-level MoE framework. The central idea of dMoE is to aggregate token-level expert distributions within each block into a unified block-level expert distribution, which is then used to guide block expert routing in a coherent manner. In this way, dMoE substantially reduces the number of uniquely activated experts during inference without sacrificing performance, thereby mitigating the memory-bound bottleneck. Extensive experiments across a variety of benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of dMoE. On average, dMoE reduces the number of uniquely activated experts from 69.5 to 16.6 while retaining 99.55% of the original performance. Meanwhile, it reduces memory usage by 74.36% to 76.78% and achieves $1.36\times$ to $2.04\times$ end-to-end latency speedup. Code is available at: https://github.com/fscdc/dMoE.
items.author: Sicheng Feng, Zigeng Chen, Gongfan Fang, Xinyin Ma, Xinchao Wang

items.title: GRUFF: LLM Pronoun Fidelity, Reasoning, and Biases in German
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.30214v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Third-person singular pronouns have long been used to study stereotypical biases in language models and to test their abilities to reason about reference. More recently, the interplay between reasoning and bias has been investigated with the task of pronoun fidelity, which assesses models' abilities to correctly reuse a previously-specified pronoun for a discourse entity, independent of other potentially distracting discourse entities mentioned in between. However, such research focuses on English, a language with limited grammatical gender and almost no gender agreement. In this paper we contribute a novel, large-scale dataset, GRUFF, to measure pronoun fidelity in German, covering four different gender agreement systems in nouns, and four sets of pronouns. With this dataset, we show that LLMs display strong grammatical agreement for masculine and feminine entities in the absence of explicit context, but not for neopronouns xier and en. In the presence of distractors, however, models degrade on all pronoun sets. Finally, we show that occupational stereotypes in this context are poorly correlated across grammatical cases and most models, except ones with closely related architectures.
items.author: Fabian Mewes, Anne Lauscher, Vagrant Gautam

items.title: StateRAG: Typed State Contracts for Complex Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.25379v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Complex retrieval-augmented generation requires evidence retrieval and control over what to retrieve next, which paths to explore, whether evidence is sufficient, and which intermediate results to retain. Existing RAG paradigms encode these decisions through method-specific model contexts, traversal procedures, verification signals, and memory. We introduce StateRAG, which represents retrieval control as a typed state external to the final reader. The state records the query plan, typed traversal path, candidate evidence, verification verdict, and reusable artifacts, with defined field semantics and designated update sources. Ordered role operators propose field values, and the controller validates and commits accepted proposals. A one-time compact-evidence check may select Bypass. Otherwise, the controller combines the committed verdict with the remaining budget to select Release, Revise, or Fallback. The final reader is invoked only after a terminal action and at most once per query. Among the evaluated methods, StateRAG achieves the best score on 10 of 11 reported quality metrics across LongBench, QASPER, and DocVQA. Its LongBench macro-average EM and F1 exceed ReAct by 6.3 and 6.1 percentage points, and its largest task-level gain is 9.8 F1 points on MuSiQue. Under normalized model-size weighting, StateRAG records lower mean LLM-token use per query than ReAct across all five workloads. In a matched LongBench control, the typed, role-owned carrier exceeds a free-form shared carrier by 1.3, 2.2, and 3.0 percentage points in macro EM, F1, and accuracy, with 6.2% lower mean RET. Removing TAM, MARS, or SMP lowers every reported LongBench and QASPER ablation metric.
items.author: Miaohe Niu, Pengxiang Li, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao

items.title: Contexting as Recommendation: Evolutionary Collaborative Filtering for Context Engineering
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.15721v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are highly sensitive to their input contexts, motivating the development of automated context engineering. However, existing methods predominantly treat this as a global search problem, seeking a single context strategy that maximizes average performance across a dataset. This restrictive assumption overlooks the fact that different inputs often require distinct guidance, leaving substantial instance-level performance gains untapped. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift by formulating context engineering as a recommendation problem. We introduce \textbf{Neural Collaborative Context Engineering (NCCE)}, a framework that transitions optimization from a static global search to dynamic, instance-wise routing. NCCE first bootstraps a diverse catalog of anchor contexts and then employs a novel \textbf{Context-CF Co-Evolution} mechanism. This stage establishes a synergistic feedback loop: a lightweight Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF) model learns instance-context preferences to guide the generation of specialized context variants, while the newly evaluated contexts continuously refine the NCF model's understanding of latent preferences. At inference time, the trained NCF model acts as a context router, dynamically assigning the most suitable context strategy to each unseen instance. Theoretical Proofs and comprehensive experiments demonstrate that by matching individual inputs with their optimal contexts, NCCE significantly improves task accuracy, highlighting the critical importance of personalization in LLM context engineering.
items.author: Jiachen Zhu, Zhuoying Ou, Congmin Zheng, Yuxiang Chen, Zeyu Zheng, Rong Shan, Lingyu Yang, Lionel Z. Wang, Weiwen Liu, Yong Yu, Weinan Zhang, Jianghao Lin

items.title: How to Train Your Latent Diffusion Language Model Jointly With the Latent Space
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.07933v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Latent diffusion models offer an attractive alternative to discrete diffusion for non-autoregressive text generation by operating on continuous text representations and denoising entire sequences in parallel. The major challenge in latent diffusion modeling is constructing a suitable latent space. In this work, we present the Latent Diffusion Language Model (LDLM), in which the latent encoder, diffusion model, and decoder are trained jointly. LDLM builds its latent space by reshaping the representations of a pre-trained language model with a trainable encoder, yielding latents that are easy to both denoise and decode into tokens. We show that naive joint training produces a low-quality diffusion model, and propose a simple training recipe consisting of an MSE decoder loss, diffusion-to-encoder warmup, adaptive timestep sampling, and decoder-input noise. Ablations show that each component substantially impacts generation performance. On OpenWebText and LM1B, LDLM achieves better generation performance than existing discrete and continuous diffusion language models while being $2{\text -}13\times$ faster, indicating that jointly learning the latent space is a key step toward making latent diffusion competitive for text generation.
items.author: Viacheslav Meshchaninov, Alexander Shabalin, Egor Chimbulatov, Nikita Gushchin, Ilya Koziev, Alexander Korotin, Dmitry Vetrov

items.title: DAWN: Dependency-Aware Fast Inference for Diffusion LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.06953v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have shown advantages in text generation, particularly due to their inherent ability for parallel decoding. However, constrained by the quality--speed trade-off, existing inference solutions adopt conservative parallel strategies, leaving substantial efficiency potential underexplored. A core challenge is that parallel decoding assumes each position can be filled independently, but tokens are often semantically coupled. Thus, the correct choice at one position constrains valid choices at others. Without modeling these positional dependencies, parallel strategies produce deteriorated outputs. Motivated by this insight, we propose DAWN, a training-free, dependency-aware decoding method for fast dLLM inference. DAWN extracts dependency relations and leverages two key observations: (1) masked positions dependent on unmasked certain positions become more reliable; (2) coupled masked positions strongly influence each other's predictions. Given those findings, DAWN leverages a dependency graph to select more reliable unmasking positions at each iteration, achieving high parallelism with negligible loss in generation quality. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets demonstrate that DAWN speedups the inference by 1.80-8.06x over baselines while preserving the generation quality. Code is released at https://github.com/lizhuo-luo/DAWN.
items.author: Lizhuo Luo, Zhuoran Shi, Jiajun Luo, Zhi Wang, Shen Ren, Wenya Wang, Tianwei Zhang

items.title: Fix the Structural Bottleneck: Context Compression via Explicit Information Transmission
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.03784v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long-context LLM agents often struggle with growing token, memory, and latency costs, making efficient context compression essential for practical deployment. Existing LLM-as-a-compressor methods remain noticeably inferior to using the full context. We find that this gap partly stems from their inability to preserve contextual information effectively. In this work, we revisit context compression from a structural perspective and identify two key bottlenecks in standard LLM-based compressors: limited coordination among compression tokens during information aggregation, and layerwise dilution that weakens useful signals from intermediate hidden states. To address these limitations, we propose ComprExIT, a new context compression framework based on explicit information transmission. ComprExIT adaptively selects features across frozen LLM layers, then allocates information from anchors to compression slots through a globally coordinated transport plan. Experiments on 12 datasets show that ComprExIT consistently outperforms strong soft-compression baselines, improving average F1 by up to 18.5%, while adding only ~1% trainable parameters and achieving more than 2x faster compression than the fastest baselines. The code will be released upon acceptance.
items.author: Jiangnan Ye, Hanqi Yan, Zhenyi Shen, Heng Chang, Ye Mao, Yulan He

items.title: HAPS: Hierarchical LLM Routing with Joint Architecture and Parameter Search
items.summary:
arXiv:2601.05903v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) routing aims to exploit the specialized strengths of different LLMs for diverse tasks. However, existing approaches typically focus only on selecting LLM architectures, treating candidate models as fixed while overlooking parameter adaptation, which can substantially affect task performance. In this paper, we introduce HAPS, a hierarchical LLM routing framework that jointly searches over model architectures and parameters. Specifically, a high-level router selects among candidate LLM architectures, while a low-level router generates input-conditioned LoRA parameters for the selected architecture, expanding each candidate from a single fixed behavior into a region of reachable behaviors. The low-level router is built on the backbone of the high-level router, so that architecture selection and parameter generation share a common representation of the prompt. We further optimize the whole framework with a reinforcement learning objective. Extensive experiments show that HAPS consistently outperforms strong routing baselines across reasoning- and knowledge-intensive benchmarks, with analyses of its components, design choices, scalability, cost, and mixed open- and closed-source deployment further demonstrating the robustness of these gains. Our code is available at https://github.com/zihangtian/HAPS.
items.author: Zihang Tian, Rui Li, Jingsen Zhang, Xiaohe Bo, Wei Huo, Xu Chen

items.title: Latent Refinement Decoding: Enhancing Diffusion-Based Language Models by Refining Belief States
items.summary:
arXiv:2510.11052v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models remain the dominant paradigm for natural language generation, but their strictly sequential decoding process leads to high inference latency. Recent diffusion-inspired language models, such as LLaDA and Dream, alleviate this issue through parallel generation, yet they still face two key limitations: information loss, since predictive distributions over non-finalised tokens are discarded at each step, and unstable commitment dynamics, where local token decisions are not sufficiently coordinated at the global level. We propose Latent Refinement Decoding (LRD), a two-stage decoding framework consisting of Latent Refinement and a Predictive Feedback Loop. In the first stage, LRD keeps masked positions as distributional mixtures of predicted tokens and the mask embedding, enabling the model to form more globally consistent beliefs before committing tokens. In the second stage, LRD progressively finalises confident tokens while preserving uncertain ones for further iterative refinement, with KL-divergence dynamics serving as a stable criterion for convergence and early stopping. Experiments show that LRD improves performance on both coding tasks, including HumanEval by 6.3 and MBPP by 2.6, and reasoning tasks, including GSM8K by 2.9 and MATH500 by 3.8, while achieving up to 10.6x overall speedup. Moreover, LRD is compatible with single-token decoding, multi-token threshold commitment, and system-level accelerators; when combined with Fast-dLLM, it reaches up to 18.4x speedup over vanilla decoding while further improving accuracy.
items.author: Qinglin Zhu, Yizhen Yao, Runcong Zhao, Yanzheng Xiang, Siya Qi, Amrutha Saseendran, Chen Jin, Philip Teare, Bin Liang, Yulan He, Lin Gui

items.title: When Guessing is Rewarded: Rethinking Language Model Evaluation with Distributional Uncertainty Scoring
items.summary:
arXiv:2510.04302v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Standard language model evaluation assigns scores to single predicted answers, rewarding high-confidence responses regardless of how residual probability mass is distributed over alternative options. This creates a systematic pressure toward overconfident guessing: under accuracy-based schemes, a model maximises its expected score by always committing to an answer rather than abstaining, even when its uncertainty is high. While penalty-based approaches partially address this by raising the confidence threshold for strategic guessing, they still treat all sub-threshold responses identically, ignoring a fundamental distinction in how models can express uncertainty - for example between hedging toward incorrect answers versus hedging toward "I don't know" responses. This paper introduces a novel evaluation metric to solve this problem of not considering a model's entire probability distribution over answer choices. The metric naturally distinguishes between harmful overconfidence in wrong answers and uncertainty expressed through abstention, providing scores in an interpretable default range. Through theoretical analysis and illustrative examples, the metric is shown to offer a more nuanced and aligned evaluation paradigm that incentivises models to express genuine uncertainty rather than guessing. Adapting 12 existing evaluation benchmarks to the metric's variants and measuring performance on six language models shows that for half of the tested benchmarks scores are negative across all tested models, indicating significant tendencies towards hallucination.
items.author: Thomas F Burns

items.title: Stabilizing Knowledge, Promoting Reasoning: Dual-Token Constraints for RLVR
items.summary:
arXiv:2507.15778v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become an effective post-training method for improving the reasoning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing methods mainly apply uniform optimization constraints across all tokens, ignoring their heterogeneous roles. Prior work shows that high-entropy tokens are closely tied to reasoning, while low-entropy tokens primarily encode factual knowledge, and recent approaches attempt to exploit this distinction by isolating token updates via masking or asynchronous training. We argue that retaining training signals across token types can lead to more effective learning. To address this, we propose Archer, an entropy-aware RLVR framework with dual-token constraints that preserves joint optimization while modulating update strength across token types. Our method introduces response-level entropy normalization for stable token classification and applies differentiated clipping ranges and KL regularization to encourage exploration on reasoning tokens while preserving knowledge tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Archer consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple model scales, improving both pass@1 and pass@K performance. These results highlight the importance of respecting sequence-level dependencies when designing fine-grained RL optimization strategies for LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/wizard-III/ArcherCodeR.
items.author: Runze Liu, Jiakang Wang, Fuzheng Zhang, Xiu Li, Guorui Zhou, Kun Gai, Ling Pan

items.title: EMERGE: A Benchmark for Updating Knowledge Graphs with Emerging Textual Knowledge
items.summary:
arXiv:2507.03617v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are structured knowledge repositories containing entities and relations between them. In this paper, we study the problem of automatically updating KGs over time in response to evolving knowledge in unstructured textual sources. Addressing this problem requires identifying a wide range of update operations based on the state of an existing KG at a given time and the information extracted from text. This contrasts with traditional information extraction pipelines, which extract knowledge from text independently of the current state of a KG. To address this challenge, we propose a generic and extensible pipeline that pairs textual passages with the KG edit operations they induce on a given KG snapshot. We instantiate this pipeline on the Wikidata knowledge graph and the English Wikipedia corpus to create EMERGE, a dataset of 233K Wikipedia passages associated with a total of 1.19 million KG edits across seven yearly Wikidata snapshots from 2019 to 2025. Our experimental results highlight key challenges in updating KG snapshots based on emerging textual knowledge, particularly in integrating knowledge expressed in text with the existing KG structure. We further show that KG access substantially improves executable updates and enables triple deprecation. These findings position EMERGE as a benchmark for developing methods that keep KGs up to date with emerging textual knowledge. The dataset (https://huggingface.co/datasets/klimzaporojets/emerge-benchmark) and code (https://github.com/klimzaporojets/emerge) are publicly available.
items.author: Klim Zaporojets, Daniel Daza, Edoardo Barba, Ira Assent, Roberto Navigli, Paul Groth

items.title: HARDTESTGEN: A High-Quality RL Verifier Generation Pipeline for LLM Algorithmic Coding
items.summary:
arXiv:2505.24098v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Verifiers provide important reward signals for reinforcement learning of large language models (LLMs). However, it is challenging to develop or create reliable verifiers, especially for code generation tasks. A well-disguised wrong solution program may only be detected by carefully human-written edge cases that are difficult to synthesize automatically. To address this issue, we propose HARDTESTGEN, an approach to synthesize high-quality test cases for algorithmic coding problems. We curate a comprehensive algorithmic programming dataset HARDTESTS with 26.6k problems and high-quality synthetic tests. Compared with existing tests, HARDTESTGEN tests demonstrate significantly higher accuracy in verifying LLM-generated code (+11.22 percentage points in precision, the percentage of actually correct code within the predicted correct ones). We also show that downstream post-training -- including rejection sampling and reinforcement learning (RL) -- using HARDTESTS verifier results in improved performance of LLM code generation. We open-source our dataset and synthesis pipeline at https://leililab.github.io/HardTests/.
items.author: Zhongmou He, Yee Man Choi, Kexun Zhang, Jiabao Ji, Junting Zhou, Dejia Xu, Ivan Bercovich, Aidan Zhang, Yixiao Zeng, Lei Li

items.title: Which Questions Improve Learning the Most? Utility Estimation of Questions with LM-based Simulations
items.summary:
arXiv:2502.17383v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Asking questions is fundamental for deeper understanding, yet evaluating and generating questions that improve downstream outcomes remains a challenging problem. To address this gap, we introduce QUEST (Question Utility Estimation with Simulated Tests), a framework that offers a new outcome-driven paradigm for question evaluation and generation, instead of indirect metrics that are based on the underlying content of the question and its answer. QUEST uses language models to simulate learners that ask questions while studying a textbook chapter and quantifies the utility of a question as its direct contribution to understanding as measured by the learner's exam performance. To analyze the effectiveness of QUEST, we curate TEXTBOOK-EXAM, a benchmark that aligns textbook sections with exam questions across five academic disciplines. Using QUEST, we filter for high-utility questions and fine-tune question generators via rejection sampling and show that questions generated by QUEST-trained models improve simulated exam scores by 18.5% compared to the next strongest baseline. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical real-world value of QUEST by showing that simulation-computed utility of a question is moderately positively correlated with its usefulness as perceived by human evaluators.
items.author: Dong-Ho Lee, Hyundong Cho, Jonathan May, Jay Pujara

items.title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12814v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Users are asking language models mental health questions and are receiving answers. We audited what 41 language models recommend to users when the same clinical information reaches them from three footings: a clinician describing a patient, a caregiver describing a loved one, or a person describing themselves. Across 19 case vignettes and five questions, we collected 35,055 free-text responses, extracted every intervention named with a validated judge, and had 29 models rate the full option lists on a seven-point Likert scale for the same cases. Models largely recommend what they rate well, with recommendation behavior differing by footing, and many models offering clinicians a consultation-style response and lay users hedged, simplified advice. When asked about recommendations for a specific intervention type, models more often named options they themselves rated below zero as initial choices, usually with conditions attached. We will release the instrument, code, and full corpus on publication as a living audit.
items.author: Matthew Flathers, Jill Noorily, Phuong Anh Nguyen, Mark Kalinich, Mina Fallah, Victoria Lisowski, Christine Shi, Rebekah M. Bodner, Anna Simms, Mihika Hete, Meiting Chen, Samuel K. Powell, Tatum Williamson, Laura Ospina-Pinillos, Haruka Notsu, Julian Herpertz, John Torous

items.title: Type-logical grammars and formal languages
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12618v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We show that type-logical grammars with the standard rules for product, associativity, extraction and infixation have an NP-complete fixed recognition problem, adapting a construction for first-order linear logic from Pshenitsyn (2025), who already showed that grammars in first-order linear logic are closed under intersection and therefore not semilinear and not mildly context-sensitive. We strengthen these results and shown that grammars in first-order linear logic can simulate the quasi-linear grammars of Book \& Greibach (1970), the grammars recognised in non-deterministic linear time (NSPACE(n) or. NLIN). I argue that NLIN is an interesting class of formal languages as well, and a useful upper bound on the time complexity of formalisms used for natural language, just like LOGCFL is a useful upper bound on the space complexity. Taken together this means that first-order linear logic can be seen as the logic of non-deterministic linear-time string languages, graph languages and automata.
items.author: Richard Moot (LIRMM,CNRS,LIRMM | PIPL,UM)

items.title: Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12412v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and never with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.
items.author: Pekka Abrahamsson, Muhammad Waseem, Esa Karjalainen, Petrus Jussila, Henri Hansen, Jussi Rasku, Bilhanan Silverajan, Kai-Kristian Kemell

items.title: Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12269v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.
items.author: Guangyan Gan, Jiahao Li, Jiashun Wang, Lin William Cong

items.title: CHO-Bench: How Do Context Hints Affect Ad Rankings in LLM Advertising?
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11955v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: LLM advertising selects advertisements based on user conversations, where user needs may extend beyond explicit product searches. ChatGPT Ads allows advertisers to provide natural-language context hints describing what they offer, who may find it useful, and when it may be useful, as additional information for ranking advertisements across diverse user conversations. However, how to effectively construct these hints remains unclear. We formulate Context Hint Optimization (CHO) as the problem of constructing context hints to improve an advertisement's ranking under a given budget. Drawing on established marketing frameworks, we develop seven context hint generation strategies covering What, Who, and When, along with a Unified strategy that combines all seven dimensions. We introduce CHO-Bench and conduct over 1.19 million paired evaluations across five datasets using embedding-based and LLM-based rankers. Our results show that context hints improve advertisement rankings under the evaluated offline rankers. While individual strategies achieve similar average gains and Unified offers no consistent advantage, strategy differences become more pronounced under specific generation-ranking configurations, with embedding-based and LLM-based rankers favoring different information dimensions. Increasing the hint budget further improves rankings with diminishing marginal gains. These findings establish an offline benchmark for studying ad-side ranking optimization in LLM advertising and highlight opportunities for model-specific hint selection and budget-aware generation and aggregation.
items.author: Shiqi Zhang, Yang Fei, Xiaokui Xiao

items.title: Language processing in the autistic brain: A meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies across modalities and age
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11927v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Language is central to social communication, which is altered in autism, and language abilities vary widely among autistic individuals. How the autistic brain processes language is central to understanding autistic communication. Yet neuroimaging studies report inconsistent findings on how autistic brain activity is altered during language processing. We synthesized 45 fMRI and PET studies (753 autistic and 777 non-autistic participants) with seed-based d mapping with permutation of subject images (SDM-PSI). We estimated autistic and non-autistic activation and their difference with meta-regressions adjusted for each study's language modality and mean age. Autistic and non-autistic brains activated a similar left-lateralized language network. Autistic brains showed reduced activity throughout the left perisylvian cortex, from the inferior frontal gyrus to the mid superior temporal gyrus and the posterior superior temporal sulcus, and increased activity in the right temporal pole. Spoken language showed a larger autistic reduction than written language in the left mid superior temporal gyrus. Adults, but not children and adolescents, showed increased autistic activity in the right superior temporal gyrus and cuneus. Autistic language processing thus relies on the typical left-lateralized network but shows reduced leftward lateralization.
items.author: Hanlin Wu, Bei Xiao, Qingxi He

items.title: Competing Influence in LLM Populations: Budget Timing and Baseline Drift
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11867v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: When competing campaigns target a population of large language model (LLM) agents, observed opinion changes may reflect both campaign influence and changes that would occur without intervention. We study how the timing of campaign expenditure and the population's own evolution shape outcomes in a network of persona-conditioned LLM agents that exchange and revise opinions in natural language. A proponent and a challenger are tasked with generating opposing messages under equal delivery budgets, while a separate stance probe measures opinions without influencing the simulation. Across eight claims, we compare single-campaign and competitive conditions against matched no-campaign runs, and evaluate all nine combinations of early, sustained, and late spending on a reference topic. Baseline stance drift varies substantially across claims and, on some, accounts for a sizeable fraction of apparent campaign effects. After accounting for this drift, the direction of observed campaign-associated changes aligns more closely with the claim's epistemic standing than with the campaigner's assigned role. Uninfluenced populations also consistently lose stance diversity, demonstrating that directional opinion change and convergence are distinct phenomena. In networks with two opinion-segregated communities, campaigns primarily reduce differences between communities rather than diversity within them. LLM campaign agents do not always argue for their assigned positions, particularly when these conflict with established evidence.
